title: The Human Body and Health Basics
summary: Learn how body systems work, the heart, blood and breathing, food and digestion, nerves and hormones, infection and prevention, and routes into health careers.
audience: Secondary students, aspiring health workers and anyone who wants to understand their body

body.p: The human body is organised in levels. Cells are the basic units of life. Similar cells form tissues, such as muscle, nerve, epithelial and connective tissue. Tissues combine into organs, such as the heart and stomach. Organs work together in organ systems, such as the digestive and respiratory systems. Together these make up an organism.

list: Skeletal and muscular: support and movement.
Circulatory: moves blood, oxygen, nutrients and waste.
Respiratory: takes in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide.
Digestive: breaks food down and absorbs nutrients.
Nervous and endocrine: control and communication through nerve signals and hormones.
Urinary: filters blood and removes waste in urine.
Immune and lymphatic: defend against infection.
Reproductive: allows new life.

body.p: Homeostasis means keeping the internal conditions of the body steady, such as temperature, water balance and blood sugar. Most systems work through feedback. When body temperature rises, you sweat, which cools you down.

body.tip: Anatomy terms describe position: anterior is front, posterior is back, superior is above, inferior is below, and medial is toward the middle.

body.p: The heart is a muscular pump with four chambers. The right side sends blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen. The left side sends oxygenated blood to the rest of the body. Valves keep blood moving one way. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry it back, and capillaries are tiny vessels where exchange with tissues takes place.

Cardiac output is the volume of blood the heart pumps per minute. It equals heart rate times stroke volume. If heart rate is 70 beats per minute and each beat pumps 70 mL, cardiac output is 70 x 70 = 4,900 mL per minute, or about 4.9 litres per minute at rest. During exercise both values increase.

When you breathe in, the diaphragm contracts and moves down, the rib muscles lift the ribs and air flows into the lungs. In the tiny air sacs called alveoli, oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out. At rest, adults breathe about 12 to 20 times per minute.

list: Red cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin.
White cells fight infection.
Platelets help blood clot.
Plasma carries nutrients, hormones and waste.

body.p: Food provides energy and the materials for growth and repair. The main nutrients are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water. Carbohydrates are the main fuel, proteins build and repair tissue, and fats store energy and support cells. Vitamins and minerals are needed in small amounts for many functions, such as iron for blood and calcium for bones.

steps: Mouth: chewing and saliva begin breaking food down.
Stomach: acid and enzymes break down protein and kill many microbes.
Small intestine: most digestion and absorption of nutrients into the blood.
Large intestine: absorbs water and forms waste.

body.p: A balanced diet includes a variety of staple foods, vegetables, fruits, beans or other protein sources, and limits too much sugar, salt and fat. Drinking safe water, washing hands and keeping food clean help prevent disease. Body Mass Index (BMI) is weight in kg divided by height in metres squared. For a person of 70 kg and 1.75 m, BMI = 70 / (1.75 x 1.75) = 22.9. BMI is only a rough screening tool and does not suit everyone, such as growing children and very muscular people. A health worker can advise you.

The nervous system sends fast electrical signals. The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system. Nerves carry messages between it and the rest of the body. A reflex action, such as pulling your hand from a hot object, travels through the spinal cord without waiting for the brain, which makes it quick.

Hormones are chemical messengers released by glands into the blood. They act more slowly but for longer. Insulin from the pancreas lowers blood sugar. Adrenaline prepares the body for danger by raising heart rate. Growth and sex hormones control development in adolescence.

list: Sleep: teenagers usually need around 8 to 10 hours.
Physical activity improves mood and memory.
Avoid alcohol, tobacco and other drugs.
Protect your head with a helmet when riding or playing risky sports.
Talk about stress with someone you trust.

body.p: Pathogens are organisms that cause disease. Bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites spread through air, water, food, contact and insect bites. The body defends itself with barriers such as skin and stomach acid, with white blood cells and with antibodies.

A vaccine teaches the immune system to recognise a pathogen without causing the disease. When the body meets the real pathogen later, it can respond quickly. Vaccination programmes have greatly reduced deaths from diseases such as measles, polio and tetanus. Follow your national vaccination schedule and ask a health worker if you are unsure.

list: Wash hands with soap and clean water, especially before eating and after using the toilet.
Drink safe water and cook food well.
Use mosquito nets and repellents where malaria is present.
Cover coughs and sneezes and stay home when unwell.
Use condoms and get tested if you are at risk of sexually transmitted infections.
Seek medical care early for fever that does not go away, bloody stools, or difficulty breathing.

body.tip: Antibiotics work against bacteria, not viruses. Use them only when prescribed and finish the course as directed.

lessons.title: Health safety and careers in health

body.p: This course is health education, not medical advice. It cannot diagnose or treat conditions. If you or someone else is seriously ill or injured, call the local emergency number or go to the nearest health facility.

list: For a serious bleed, press firmly on the wound with clean cloth and get help.
If someone is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call for emergency help and start CPR if you are trained.
Never give medicines meant for others, and keep them out of children's reach.
Do not rely on social media for treatment. Ask a health professional.

body.p: Health professions include doctors, nurses, midwives, pharmacists, laboratory scientists, physiotherapists, radiographers, community health workers, public health officers, nutritionists and many more. Most require a certificate, diploma or degree and registration with a professional council. Entry requirements differ by country. Good preparation includes strong biology, chemistry and communication skills.

body.tip: Volunteer at a clinic, Red Cross or community health programme to see the work before you commit to a long course.
